title: Cold water
hookLine: claims for cold plunges run ahead of the evidence; go carefully

lines: A TUB OF ICE WATER, A PHONE ON A CHAIR.
cards: A tub of ice water sits in someone's backyard, a phone propped on a chair to film it. In they go, gasping, grinning for the camera.

The videos promise a great deal: more energy, a brighter mood, a stronger immune system, a sharper mind, burned fat. Some of that may turn out to be partly true. A lot of it is out ahead of the studies.
Today: a popular trend, an old Roman who loved cold water, and the plain virtue of going carefully.

teach.b: First, what's well known. Cold water is a shock to the body. Sudden cold can trigger a gasp and fast breathing, and the heart works hard.

That's why sudden immersion in cold water is dangerous for swimmers, and why people with heart conditions are told to ask a doctor before trying it. Second, what's claimed: mood, immunity, weight, focus, recovery.

teach.h: THE STUDIES ARE SMALL SO FAR.
teach.b: There are studies, but so far they tend to be small and short, and they don't add up to the promises in the videos. Some findings may hold up; it's too early to say which. Third, an old enthusiast.

Seneca, the Roman philosopher this path met in its first month, calls himself, in one of his letters to his friend Lucilius, a great devotee of cold water, who used to greet the new year with a plunge.
Then he admits that age changed things: first he moved his plunges to the river Tiber, then to a tub warmed by the sun. He tells it with a smile at himself. The cold-water lover learned to adjust.
Anyone curious can start small, with a cool finish to a shower.
Never plunge alone in open water. Get out when shivering gets strong or the skin goes numb. Ask a doctor first if the heart isn't strong.
And it's perfectly fine to skip a trend altogether.

how: People who take up cold water often begin with cool showers, swim in groups rather than alone, and get medical advice first if they have heart problems.

games.q: you're Seneca, a lifelong lover of cold plunges, and you're getting older. what do you do?
o: keep plunging into the coldest water you can find.
move to the Tiber, then to a sun-warmed tub.
games.why: in his letter, Seneca says he adjusted step by step, and tells it with a smile at himself.

practice: Notice the air on your face and hands, cool or warm, and the place where your body meets the chair, usually a little warmer. Notice your breath, cooler coming in, warmer going out; no plunge needed.
Then think of one wellness trend that's been tugging at you, and let yourself set it down for now, or until the evidence is clearer.

wordCard.voice: Cold water. A real shock to the body, with claims that run ahead of small studies. Seneca loved it, and learned to adjust. Today's word.

orig.note: a Greek word Seneca uses in his Latin letter: a cold-water bather.

carryVoice: Your line: careful. Even Seneca, who loved the cold, learned to adjust. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.ref: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 83
